blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Coal and petroleum are fossil fuels formed over millions of years from the buried remains of plants and marine organisms under high pressure and temperature.
Coal processing yields valuable by-products including coke (almost pure carbon), coal tar (mixture of aromatic substances), and coal gas.
Petroleum (crude oil) is separated into various fractions like petrol, diesel, kerosene, paraffin wax, and LPG via fractional distillation.
Pollution is defined as the introduction of harmful contaminants into the natural environment, causing adverse changes to ecosystems and human health.

blocks.content:
Coal and petroleum are very important natural resources that are used by human beings in daily life.

They provide energy for cooking, transportation, industries and electricity generation.

Without these resources, modern life would not be possible.

These resources are found deep inside the earth and were formed millions of years ago.

Because they are formed from the remains of plants and animals, they are called fossil fuels.
2. FOSSIL FUELS

Fossil fuels are fuels that are formed from the dead remains of plants and animals.

Millions of years ago, plants and animals died and got buried under layers of soil and rocks.

Due to very high temperature and pressure inside the earth, these remains slowly changed into coal, petroleum and natural gas.

Since this process takes millions of years, fossil fuels cannot be formed again quickly.

Therefore, fossil fuels are called non‑renewable resources.
3. IMPORTANCE OF FOSSIL FUELS

Fossil fuels are extremely important for human life.

They are used to generate electricity in thermal power plants.

They are used as fuel in vehicles such as cars, buses and trains.

They are also used as raw materials in many industries such as plastic, chemical and fertilizer industries.

Without fossil fuels, industries and transportation would stop.
4. COAL

Coal is a black or brownish‑black solid substance.

It mainly contains carbon along with small amounts of hydrogen, oxygen and sulphur.

Coal is one of the oldest fuels used by human beings.
It is mainly used to generate electricity and in the manufacture of iron and steel.
5. TYPES OF COAL

Coal is found in different forms depending on the amount of carbon present in it.

The four main types of coal are:

Peat, Lignite, Bituminous coal and Anthracite.

Anthracite contains the highest amount of carbon and gives maximum heat.
6. DESTRUCTIVE DISTILLATION OF COAL

When coal is heated strongly in the absence of air, it breaks down into useful substances.

This process is called destructive distillation of coal.

During this process, coal is converted into three main products: coke, coal tar and coal gas.
7. COKE

Coke is a hard, porous and black substance.

It is almost pure carbon.

Because of its high carbon content, coke burns with very high heat.

Coke is used as a fuel and as a reducing agent in the extraction of metals such as iron.

It is also used in the manufacture of steel.

items:
Coal tar is a thick, black liquid with a strong smell.

It is a mixture of many useful chemical substances.

Coal tar is used for making roads, dyes, medicines, naphthalene, plastics and synthetic fibres.

It is also used for waterproofing roofs.

blocks.content: 9. COAL GAS

Coal gas is a gaseous fuel obtained during the processing of coal.

It burns with a clean flame and produces a large amount of heat.

Coal gas is used as a fuel for heating and lighting.
10. PETROLEUM

Petroleum is a dark, oily liquid found deep under the earth.

It is also known as crude oil.

Petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons.

Because of its great commercial value, petroleum is called black gold.
11. REFINING OF PETROLEUM

Petroleum is refined in a petroleum refinery by a process called fractional distillation.

In this process, crude oil is heated and separated into different fractions based on their boiling points.

Each fraction has a specific use.
12. FRACTIONS OF PETROLEUM

The important fractions of petroleum include:

Petroleum gas used for cooking,

Petrol used in vehicles,

Kerosene used in stoves and aircrafts,

Diesel used in buses and generators,

Lubricating oil used in machines,

Paraffin wax used in candles and ointments,

Bitumen used for road construction.
13. NATURAL GAS

Natural gas is the cleanest fossil fuel.

It produces very little pollution.

It is used for cooking, electricity generation and as CNG in vehicles.

Because it burns completely, it is considered an environment‑friendly fuel.
14. CONSERVATION OF FOSSIL FUELS

Fossil fuels are limited in quantity and take millions of years to form.

Their excessive use leads to pollution and global warming.

Therefore, it is important to conserve fossil fuels.

This can be done by using renewable sources of energy and avoiding wastage.
15. ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF FOSSIL FUELS

Burning of fossil fuels releases harmful gases such as carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide.

These gases cause air pollution, acid rain and global warming.

Continuous use of fossil fuels also leads to climate change.
16. IMPORTANT EXAM POINTS

Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels.

Coke is almost pure carbon.

Petroleum is called black gold.

Natural gas is the cleanest fossil fuel.

Coal tar is used for road construction.

Petroleum is refined by fractional distillation.
17. QUICK REVISION

Coal and petroleum are non‑renewable natural resources.

Coal gives coke, coal tar and coal gas.

Petroleum is refined to obtain useful products.

Natural gas is the cleanest fuel.

Fossil fuels should be conserved for future generations.
CHAPTER 9 : COMBUSTION AND FLAME
1. INTRODUCTION

Combustion is a very common process that we observe in our daily life.

Whenever a substance burns and produces heat and light, the process is called combustion.

Examples of combustion include burning of wood, coal, petrol, LPG and candles.

Combustion plays a very important role in cooking, transportation and industries.
2. COMBUSTION

Combustion is a chemical process in which a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat and light.

The substance that undergoes combustion is called a combustible substance.

Oxygen is necessary for combustion to take place.

Without oxygen, combustion cannot occur.
3. CONDITIONS NECESSARY FOR COMBUSTION

For combustion to occur, three essential conditions must be satisfied.

First, there must be a combustible substance.

Second, there must be sufficient supply of oxygen.

Third, the substance must be heated to its ignition temperature.

If any one of these conditions is absent, combustion will not take place.
4. IGNITION TEMPERATURE

The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire and starts burning is called its ignition temperature.

Different substances have different ignition temperatures.

Substances with low ignition temperature catch fire easily.

Petrol has a very low ignition temperature and hence catches fire easily.
5. TYPES OF COMBUSTION

There are different types of combustion based on how a substance burns.

The main types are rapid combustion, spontaneous combustion and explosive combustion.
5.1 RAPID COMBUSTION

Rapid combustion is a type of combustion in which a substance burns quickly when a flame is applied.

It produces heat and light immediately.

Example: Burning of LPG in a gas stove.
5.2 SPONTANEOUS COMBUSTION

Spontaneous combustion is a type of combustion in which a substance catches fire on its own without any external flame.

This happens due to rise in temperature inside the substance.

Example: White phosphorus catches fire on its own.
5.3 EXPLOSIVE COMBUSTION

Explosive combustion is a type of combustion in which a large amount of gas and heat are produced suddenly.

This results in an explosion.

Example: Bursting of crackers and explosions of bombs.

A flame is the visible, glowing part of a fire.

It is produced when a combustible substance burns in the gaseous state.

Not all substances produce a flame while burning.

For example, charcoal does not produce a flame.

A flame has different zones based on temperature and combustion.

The three main zones of a flame are:

Inner zone, middle zone and outer zone.
7.1 INNER ZONE

The inner zone is the darkest part of the flame.

It consists of unburnt vapours of the fuel.

This zone is the least hot part of the flame.
7.2 MIDDLE ZONE

The middle zone is the luminous part of the flame.

It is yellow in colour.

It is moderately hot and produces soot particles.
7.3 OUTER ZONE

The outer zone is the hottest part of the flame.

It is blue in colour.

Complete combustion takes place in this zone.
8. FUELS

A fuel is a substance that produces useful energy on burning.

Fuels are used for cooking, heating, transportation and electricity generation.

Examples of fuels include wood, coal, petrol, diesel and LPG.
9. CALORIFIC VALUE

The amount of heat produced by burning 1 kg of a fuel is called its calorific value.

It is expressed in kilojoule per kilogram (kJ/kg).

A good fuel has a high calorific value.

A good fuel should have high calorific value.

It should be cheap and easily available.

It should burn easily and produce less smoke.

It should not leave behind harmful residues.
11. CONTROL OF FIRE

Fire can be controlled by removing any one of the three essential requirements of combustion.

Fire can be controlled by cooling, cutting off oxygen supply or removing the fuel.

Fire extinguishers are used to put out fires.
12. HARMFUL EFFECTS OF BURNING FUELS

Burning of fuels releases harmful gases such as carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.

These gases cause air pollution and global warming.

Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide which is very poisonous.

Combustion is a chemical process.

Oxygen is necessary for combustion.

Ignition temperature is the minimum temperature required to start burning.

The outer zone of flame is the hottest.

Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas.
14. QUICK REVISION

Combustion is the process of burning.

Three conditions are required for combustion.

Flame has three zones.

Fuels have calorific value.

Fire can be controlled by removing heat, oxygen or fuel.
CHAPTER 10 : CONSERVATION OF NATURAL RESOURCES
1. INTRODUCTION

Natural resources are the resources that are obtained from nature.

These resources are very important for the survival of human beings and other living organisms.

Examples of natural resources include air, water, soil, forests, minerals, coal, petroleum and natural gas.

Since these resources are limited in nature, they must be used carefully and wisely.

The protection and proper use of natural resources is called conservation of natural resources.
2. TYPES OF NATURAL RESOURCES

Natural resources are mainly of two types: renewable resources and non-renewable resources.

Renewable resources are those which can be replenished naturally in a short period of time.

Non-renewable resources are those which take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced easily.
3. RENEWABLE RESOURCES

Renewable resources are resources that can be reused or replenished by natural processes.

Examples of renewable resources include air, water, sunlight, wind and forests.

These resources are not exhausted easily if used carefully.

However, overuse can also lead to their depletion.
4. NON-RENEWABLE RESOURCES

Non-renewable resources are resources that cannot be replaced once they are exhausted.

Examples include coal, petroleum, natural gas and minerals.

These resources take millions of years to form and therefore must be used very carefully.
5. FORESTS

Forests are one of the most important natural resources.

They provide oxygen, food, shelter and raw materials.

Forests help in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

They also prevent soil erosion and help in maintaining rainfall.
6. CONSERVATION OF FORESTS

Deforestation leads to many environmental problems such as floods, droughts and loss of biodiversity.

Therefore, forests should be conserved.

Planting more trees, avoiding unnecessary cutting of trees and afforestation help in conservation of forests.
7. WILDLIFE

Wildlife includes animals, birds and insects found in forests and natural habitats.

Wildlife plays an important role in maintaining ecological balance.

Due to hunting, deforestation and pollution, many animals are becoming endangered.
CHAPTER 8 : COAL AND PETROLEUM
8. CONSERVATION OF WILDLIFE

Wildlife should be protected to maintain balance in nature.

National parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves are created for wildlife conservation.

Hunting and poaching of animals should be strictly prohibited.
9.WATER RESOURCES

Water is one of the most important natural resources.

It is essential for drinking, agriculture, industries and daily activities.

Fresh water is limited and should be conserved.

Rainwater harvesting is an important method to save water.
10. COAL AND PETROLEUM AS RESOURCES

Coal and petroleum are non-renewable natural resources.

They are used as fuels and also as raw materials in industries.

Their excessive use leads to pollution and depletion.

Therefore, they should be used carefully.
11. NEED FOR CONSERVATION OF RESOURCES

Natural resources are limited and are being used rapidly due to increasing population.

If resources are not conserved, future generations will suffer.

Conservation helps in maintaining ecological balance and sustainable development.
12. SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT

Sustainable development means using natural resources in such a way that they are available for future generations.

It focuses on development without harming the environment.

Using renewable energy and reducing waste are important steps toward sustainable development.
13. FIVE Rs OF CONSERVATION

The five Rs are Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose and Recycle.

These principles help in reducing waste and conserving natural resources.

Following the five Rs helps in protecting the environment.
14. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT OF RESOURCE EXPLOITATION

Excessive use of natural resources leads to deforestation, pollution, climate change and loss of biodiversity.

It also causes global warming and scarcity of resources.

Therefore, responsible use of resources is very important.
15. IMPORTANT EXAM POINTS

Natural resources are of two types: renewable and non-renewable.

Forests help in maintaining ecological balance.

Coal and petroleum are non-renewable resources.

Wildlife conservation is necessary to maintain biodiversity.

Sustainable development is necessary for future generations.
16. QUICK REVISION

Natural resources are gifts of nature.

They should be conserved for future generations.

Forests, water and wildlife need protection.

Non-renewable resources must be used carefully.

Sustainable development ensures balanced use of resources.
CHAPTER 11 : SOURCES OF ENERGY
1. INTRODUCTION

Energy is the capacity to do work. Every activity in our daily life requires energy.

From cooking food to running vehicles and operating machines, energy is required everywhere.

Energy plays a vital role in the economic development of a country.

The sources from which we obtain energy are called sources of energy.
2. IMPORTANCE OF ENERGY

Energy is required for domestic, industrial and commercial purposes.

It is used in homes for cooking, lighting and heating.

Industries use energy to run machines and produce goods.

Transportation also depends on energy in the form of petrol, diesel and electricity.

Without energy, modern life would not be possible.
3. CLASSIFICATION OF SOURCES OF ENERGY

Sources of energy are broadly classified into two types:

1. Renewable sources of energy

2. Non-renewable sources of energy

This classification is based on their availability and renewability.
4. RENEWABLE SOURCES OF ENERGY

Renewable sources of energy are those sources which can be replenished naturally in a short period of time.

These sources are environment-friendly and do not cause pollution.

Examples include solar energy, wind energy, water energy and biomass.
5. SOLAR ENERGY

Solar energy is obtained from the Sun.

It is the most abundant and inexhaustible source of energy.

Solar energy is converted into electrical energy using solar panels.

It is used for cooking, heating water, lighting homes and generating electricity.

Solar energy does not produce pollution and is free of cost.
6. WIND ENERGY

Wind energy is obtained from the movement of air.

Windmills are used to convert wind energy into electrical energy.

Wind energy is clean, renewable and does not pollute the environment.

However, it depends on wind speed and location.
7. HYDROELECTRIC ENERGY

Hydroelectric energy is obtained from flowing or falling water.

Dams are constructed on rivers to store water at a height.

When water flows down, it rotates turbines which generate electricity.

Hydroelectric power is renewable and pollution-free.
8. BIOMASS ENERGY

Biomass energy is obtained from plant and animal waste.

Examples include wood, cow dung, agricultural waste and biogas.

Biogas is produced from biomass in biogas plants and is used for cooking and lighting.

Biomass energy helps in waste management and reduces pollution.
9. NON-RENEWABLE SOURCES OF ENERGY

Non-renewable sources of energy are those which cannot be replaced once exhausted.

These sources take millions of years to form.

Examples include coal, petroleum and natural gas.

They are limited in quantity and will get exhausted in the future.
10. FOSSIL FUELS

Fossil fuels include coal, petroleum and natural gas.

They are formed from dead plants and animals buried under the earth for millions of years.

Fossil fuels are widely used for electricity generation and transportation.

However, their excessive use causes pollution and global warming.
11. THERMAL POWER PLANTS

Thermal power plants produce electricity by burning coal.

The heat produced converts water into steam.

The steam rotates turbines which generate electricity.

Thermal power plants are the major source of electricity in India.
12. NUCLEAR ENERGY

Nuclear energy is obtained by splitting the nucleus of radioactive elements such as uranium.

This process is called nuclear fission.

A large amount of energy is produced from a small amount of fuel.

However, nuclear energy produces radioactive waste which is harmful.
13. ADVANTAGES OF RENEWABLE ENERGY

Renewable sources of energy are environment-friendly.

They do not produce harmful gases.

They are inexhaustible and available in large quantity.

They reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

blocks.content: 14. DISADVANTAGES OF NON-RENEWABLE ENERGY

Non-renewable sources of energy cause air pollution.

They release greenhouse gases leading to global warming.

They are limited and will be exhausted in future.
15. CONSERVATION OF ENERGY

Energy should be conserved to ensure availability for future generations.

We should use energy efficiently and avoid wastage.

Using renewable energy sources helps in conserving non-renewable energy.
16. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT OF ENERGY USE

Excessive use of fossil fuels leads to air pollution, global warming and climate change.

Acid rain is caused due to emission of sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.

Therefore, clean and renewable sources of energy should be promoted.
17. IMPORTANT EXAM POINTS

Energy is the capacity to do work.

Solar energy is the cleanest source of energy.

Coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable.

Hydroelectric power is renewable.

Nuclear energy produces large amount of energy.
18. QUICK REVISION

Energy is required for all activities.

Sources of energy are renewable and non-renewable.

Solar, wind and water are renewable sources.

Coal and petroleum are non-renewable.

Energy conservation is very important.
CHAPTER 13 : SYNTHETIC FIBRES AND PLASTICS
1. INTRODUCTION

Clothes are one of the basic needs of human beings.

In earlier times, people used natural fibres like cotton, wool and silk for making clothes.

With the advancement of science and technology, synthetic fibres were developed.

Synthetic fibres are man-made fibres prepared from chemical substances.

They are widely used today because they are strong, cheap and durable.
2. FIBRES

A fibre is a thin, thread-like structure which can be woven to make fabrics.

Fibres are broadly classified into two types: natural fibres and synthetic fibres.

Natural fibres are obtained from plants and animals, while synthetic fibres are made by humans.
3. NATURAL FIBRES

Natural fibres are obtained from plants and animals.

Cotton is obtained from cotton plants.

Wool is obtained from sheep.

Silk is obtained from silkworms.

Natural fibres are biodegradable and environment-friendly.
4. SYNTHETIC FIBRES

Synthetic fibres are man-made fibres prepared from chemical substances called polymers.

They are made in factories using chemical processes.

Synthetic fibres are strong, durable and easy to maintain.
5. TYPES OF SYNTHETIC FIBRES

There are mainly three types of synthetic fibres:

Rayon, Nylon, Polyester and Acrylic.

Each type has different properties and uses.
6. RAYON

Rayon is called artificial silk because it resembles silk in appearance.

It is made from cellulose obtained from wood pulp.

Rayon is soft, comfortable and used in making clothes, curtains and bed sheets.
7. NYLON

Nylon was the first fully synthetic fibre.

It is very strong, elastic and lightweight.

Nylon is used to make ropes, parachutes, toothbrush bristles and fishing nets.
8. POLYESTER

Polyester is a synthetic fibre that does not wrinkle easily.

It is strong, lightweight and easy to wash.

Terylene and PET are examples of polyester.

Polyester is used to make clothes, bottles and packaging materials.
9. ACRYLIC

Acrylic is a synthetic fibre that looks like wool.

It is warm, light and cheap.

Acrylic is used to make sweaters, blankets and carpets.
10. PLASTICS

Plastics are synthetic materials made from polymers.

They are lightweight, strong, durable and resistant to corrosion.

Plastics are widely used in daily life.
11. TYPES OF PLASTICS

Plastics are of two types:

Thermoplastics and Thermosetting plastics.
12. THERMOPLASTICS

Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be reshaped.

They can be reused many times.

Examples include polythene and PVC.

They are used to make toys, pipes and containers.
13. THERMOSETTING PLASTICS

Thermosetting plastics do not soften on heating.

Once moulded, they cannot be reshaped.

Examples include bakelite and melamine.

They are used in electrical switches and kitchenware.
14. PROPERTIES OF PLASTICS

Plastics are lightweight and strong.

They are non-reactive and corrosion-resistant.

They are poor conductors of heat and electricity.

Plastics are durable and long-lasting.
15.ADVANTAGES OF SYNTHETIC FIBRES AND PLASTICS

They are strong and durable.

They are lightweight and easy to carry.

They are cheaper than natural fibres.

They are resistant to chemicals and water.
16. DISADVANTAGES OF SYNTHETIC FIBRES AND PLASTICS

They are non-biodegradable and cause pollution.

They release toxic gases on burning.

They are harmful to animals if ingested.

They cause environmental problems.
17. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT

Plastic waste causes soil and water pollution.

Burning plastics releases poisonous gases.

Plastics clog drains and harm aquatic life.

Hence, plastic waste management is very important.
18. 5R PRINCIPLE

The 5R principle includes Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose and Recycle.

Following the 5R principle helps in reducing plastic waste and protecting the environment.
19. IMPORTANT EXAM POINTS

Rayon is artificial silk.

Nylon is the first synthetic fibre.

Plastics are non-biodegradable.

Thermoplastics can be reshaped.

Thermosetting plastics cannot be reshaped.
20. QUICK REVISION

Synthetic fibres are man-made fibres.

Rayon, nylon, polyester and acrylic are synthetic fibres.

Plastics are of two types: thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.

Plastic waste should be managed properly.
CHAPTER 14 : ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION
1. INTRODUCTION TO ENVIRONMENT

The environment includes all living and non-living components present around us such as air, water, soil, plants, animals and human beings.

It provides basic necessities of life like food, water, air and shelter.

A balanced environment is essential for the survival of all living organisms.

When harmful substances enter the environment and disturb this natural balance, it leads to environmental pollution.

In the modern world, environmental pollution has become a global issue due to industrialization, urbanization and overpopulation.
2. POLLUTION – MEANING AND DEFINITION

Pollution is defined as the contamination of the environment by harmful physical, chemical or biological substances.

These harmful substances are called pollutants.

Pollution degrades the quality of air, water and soil, making them unsafe for living beings.

Pollution can be natural, but most pollution today is caused by human activities.
3. TYPES OF ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION

Environmental pollution is broadly classified into the following types:

1. Air Pollution

2. Water Pollution

3. Soil Pollution

4. Noise Pollution

5. Plastic Pollution

6. Thermal Pollution

Each type of pollution affects the environment in a different manner.

CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) primarily consists of methane (CH4) and is preferred as a clean vehicle fuel due to low pollutant emissions.
Oxides of sulfur and nitrogen released by burning fossil fuels dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain (sulfuric acid and nitric acid).

blocks.content: 4. AIR POLLUTION

Air pollution occurs when harmful gases, smoke, dust and particulate matter enter the atmosphere.

Major air pollutants include carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide and particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10).

Major sources of air pollution are vehicles, industries, burning of coal, stubble burning and forest fires.

Air pollution causes respiratory diseases, lung cancer, asthma, eye irritation and reduced lung capacity.
4.1 CURRENT ISSUE – AIR QUALITY INDEX (AQI)

Air Quality Index (AQI) is used to measure the level of air pollution.

It classifies air quality into good, satisfactory, moderate, poor, very poor and severe.

Cities like Delhi, Gurugram and Kanpur often record severe AQI levels, especially during winter.

Government has introduced measures like Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) to control air pollution.
5. WATER POLLUTION

Water pollution occurs when harmful substances like industrial waste, sewage, pesticides and plastics enter water bodies.

Rivers, lakes, seas and groundwater get polluted due to human activities.

Polluted water causes diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery.

Water pollution also kills aquatic organisms and disturbs aquatic ecosystems.
5.1 CURRENT ISSUE – NAMAMI GANGE PROJECT

The Government of India launched the Namami Gange Programme to clean and rejuvenate River Ganga.

It focuses on sewage treatment, industrial waste control and river surface cleaning.

The programme aims to make river water clean and safe for use.
6. SOIL POLLUTION

Soil pollution occurs due to excessive use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides, insecticides and plastic waste.

Industrial waste and garbage dumping also contribute to soil pollution.

Soil pollution reduces soil fertility and affects crop productivity.

It also contaminates underground water.
7. PLASTIC POLLUTION

Plastic pollution is one of the biggest environmental challenges today.

Plastic is non-biodegradable and remains in the environment for hundreds of years.

Plastic waste clogs drains, harms animals and pollutes oceans.

Microplastics have now entered food chains, posing serious health risks.
7.1 CURRENT ISSUE – SINGLE USE PLASTIC BAN

India has banned single-use plastic items such as plastic bags, cups and straws.

This step aims to reduce plastic waste and promote eco-friendly alternatives.

Many states have imposed heavy fines on the use of plastic bags.
8. NOISE POLLUTION

Noise pollution is caused by unwanted loud sounds from vehicles, factories, loudspeakers and construction activities.

It causes hearing loss, stress, high blood pressure and mental disorders.

Continuous exposure to noise pollution reduces concentration and productivity.
9. GREENHOUSE EFFECT

Greenhouse effect is the process by which greenhouse gases trap heat in the Earth’s atmosphere.

Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour are major greenhouse gases.
Excess greenhouse effect leads to global warming.
10. GLOBAL WARMING

Global warming refers to the gradual increase in Earth’s average temperature.

It is mainly caused by burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.

Global warming results in melting of glaciers, rise in sea level, floods and droughts.
11. CLIMATE CHANGE

Climate change refers to long-term changes in weather patterns.

It includes changes in rainfall, temperature and seasons.

Climate change affects agriculture, biodiversity and human life.
12. OZONE LAYER DEPLETION

The ozone layer protects Earth from harmful ultraviolet rays of the Sun.

Chemicals like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage the ozone layer.

Ozone depletion leads to skin cancer, eye problems and crop damage.
12.1 MONTREAL PROTOCOL

The Montreal Protocol is an international agreement to phase out ozone-depleting substances.

India is a signatory to this agreement and has taken steps to reduce CFC emissions.
13. CONTROL OF ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION

Pollution can be controlled by using renewable energy, reducing fossil fuel consumption,

planting trees, managing waste properly and promoting recycling.

Government policies and public awareness play a major role in pollution control.
14. ROLE OF INDIVIDUAL

Every individual has a responsibility to protect the environment.

Saving electricity, conserving water, avoiding plastic and planting trees can reduce pollution.

Public participation is essential for environmental protection.
15. IMPORTANT EXAM POINTS

• AQI measures air pollution level.

• Global warming is caused by greenhouse gases.

• Plastic is non-biodegradable.

• Ozone layer protects from UV radiation.

• Namami Gange is a river cleaning programme.
16. QUICK REVISION

Environmental pollution affects air, water and soil.

Major causes are human activities and industrialization.

Pollution leads to health hazards and climate change.

Control of pollution is essential for sustainable development.
